explain.say: Wi-Fi is a radio. Your router and your phone both have radio transmitters and receivers, and they swap data by sending radio waves through the air instead of along a wire.

faq.q: How are bits put onto a radio wave?
faq.a: This is called modulation. The router changes the wave's amplitude, its strength, and its phase, its timing, and each combination stands for several bits. Wi-Fi also splits the data across many slightly different frequencies at once.
Wi-Fi mainly uses the 2.4 gigahertz and 5 gigahertz bands, and newer routers also use 6 gigahertz. A 2.4 gigahertz wave is about 12.5 centimetres long.
asks: What is the difference between 2.4 and 5 GHz Wi-Fi?

faq.q: Why is Wi-Fi slower through walls?
faq.a: Walls, floors and especially metal and water absorb and reflect radio waves, so less signal reaches your device. With a weaker signal, the router must use simpler, slower codes and resend more data.
asks: Why is my Wi-Fi weak upstairs?

faq.q: What happens if Wi-Fi data gets lost?
faq.a: Each packet is checked when it arrives, and the receiver sends a short acknowledgement. If the sender gets no reply, it sends the packet again, so nothing goes missing, it just takes longer.

faq.q: Is Wi-Fi the same as the internet?
faq.a: No. Wi-Fi is only the radio link between your device and your router. The router then connects to the internet through a cable, fibre or mobile link from your internet provider.
asks: Why do I have Wi-Fi but no internet?

facts: A 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi radio wave is about 12.5 centimetres long.
Microwave ovens work at about 2.45 GHz, which is why a running microwave can disturb 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi.

quiz.say: Which Wi-Fi band usually reaches further through walls?
quiz.why: Lower-frequency 2.4 gigahertz waves are absorbed less by walls, so they reach further.

wrong.1: 5 gigahertz carries more data but fades sooner through walls.
wrong.2: They behave differently: higher frequencies are absorbed more.
